694.title: bhakti — the Narada Bhakti Sutras opening
694.hook: four teachers are asked what bhakti looks like, and the book lets every one of them answer
694.howItsDone: In many Vaishnava homes and temples, devotion takes all four shapes the sutras name: daily puja, retelling and singing the stories of Krishna or Rama, quiet remembrance, and offering one's work to God. Groups often study a few sutras at a time with a teacher's commentary.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and the opening of the Narada Bhakti Sutras: now, then, we will explain bhakti. The definition is supreme love.

Ask four people who love someone how you can tell, and you'll get four answers. One says: they show up. One says: they can't stop talking about them. One says: they're just happy. And one says: watch what happens when they're apart. The Narada Bhakti Sutras do something like that. Having defined bhakti as supreme love, they stop and ask: what are its marks? And instead of one answer, they let four teachers speak.
screen: `HOW CAN YOU TELL SOMEONE LOVES?` → `FOUR PEOPLE, FOUR ANSWERS.` → `THE SUTRAS ASK THE SAME.`

segments.voice: Sutra fifteen sets it up: now its marks are described, according to different views. First Vyasa, son of Parashara, the sage tradition credits with the Mahabharata. For him, bhakti is fondness for worship: the lamp, the flowers, the offering. Second, Garga: fondness for talk about the Lord, the stories told and retold. Third, Shandilya: delight in the Self that nothing gets in the way of. Three teachers, three marks, and the text calls none of them wrong. Then sutra nineteen gives Narada's own view. Bhakti is offering every action to the Lord, and feeling the deepest anguish on forgetting him. The word there is vyakulata: being thrown into turmoil, unsettled, like someone who's lost a child in a crowd. Love is measured not only by what you do, but by how much it hurts to forget. Then the sutras give an example: the cowherd women of Vraja, the gopis, who loved Krishna. And they head off a misreading. Even the gopis, the text says, did not forget his greatness. Love without that would be like the love of a secret lover, who takes no joy in the beloved's joy. So at its opening, a short book on devotion makes room for several teachers before it speaks for itself. Four marks, then: the lamp and flowers, the stories, the quiet joy, and the ache. The book keeps all four.
screen: `VYASA: FONDNESS FOR WORSHIP.` · `GARGA: LOVE OF THE STORIES.` · `SHANDILYA: DELIGHT IN THE SELF.` · `NARADA: ANGUISH ON FORGETTING.` · then, large: `LIKE THE GOPIS OF VRAJA.`

segments.voice: Bring back what you love most, the one from yesterday, and try each teacher's mark lightly: a small act of care you do for it, a story about it you love to tell, a plain gladness that it exists. Then ask whether, if it slipped from your mind for a whole day, you'd feel the gap. No answer is the right one; let them come, and just breathe.
Bhakti. Devotion. Vyasa sees it in worship, Garga in the stories, Shandilya in delight, and Narada in the ache of forgetting.
Your line: the ache of forgetting. Missing something can be a kind of love. Day six hundred ninety-four, done.

695.title: jnana — Shankara's *Atmabodha*
695.hook: a short Sanskrit poem says action can't remove ignorance, any more than sweeping can remove the dark
695.carry: light, not sweeping, ends the dark
695.howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta circles, the Atmabodha is often among the first texts a student reads with a teacher, verse by verse, alongside listening, reflection and meditation on the teaching. Students often combine study like this with work done as service and with devotion.

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and four teachers in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: worship, the stories, delight, and Narada's own mark, the ache of forgetting.

A dark room, at night. You could sweep it, scrub the floor, rearrange the furniture, work there all night. None of it removes the dark. One thing does, and it takes no effort at all: the light. That picture sits near the beginning of a short Sanskrit poem called the Atmabodha, knowledge of the Self, which tradition gives to Shankara. After karma, the path of action, and bhakti, the path of love, here is the third strand: jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A DARK ROOM.` → `SWEEPING WON'T HELP.` → `THE THIRD STRAND: JNANA.`

segments.voice: The Atmabodha is short, a kind of pocket handbook of Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the Self and Brahman are not two. Tradition credits it to Shankara; some scholars question whether he wrote it, and it's often studied as a beginner's text. The first verse says who it's for: people whose faults have been worn down by discipline, who are calm, free of craving, and long for freedom. So it starts where the karma days left off: a disciplined life has already prepared the mind. The second verse makes its claim. Just as fire is what actually cooks the food, knowledge, not any other practice, is what directly brings liberation. Verse three gives the reason. Action isn't opposed to ignorance, so it can't destroy it. Knowledge is opposed to it, the way light is opposed to darkness. And verse four: because of ignorance, the Self seems limited; when ignorance goes, the Self shines on its own, like the sun when the clouds pass. Jnana means knowing, from the root jna, to know, but not collecting facts. It's closer to the moment you see that the thing you feared was never there. Here the schools of Vedanta take different roads. Shankara's school holds that knowledge alone liberates, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Teachers in Ramanuja's tradition hold that devotion to the Lord, supported by knowledge, is the way. Both are living Hindu paths, each with its own teachers, temples and students reading verse by verse.
screen: `FOR THE CALM WHO LONG TO BE FREE.` · `FIRE COOKS; KNOWLEDGE FREES.` · `LIGHT, NOT SWEEPING, ENDS THE DARK.` · `THE SUN BEHIND THE CLOUDS.` · then, large: `JNANA: KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Notice something simple: you're aware, as sounds, thoughts and feelings in the body come and go. Don't chase any of them; rest as the one who notices, the way the sky stays while the clouds cross it. If you drift, that's fine; noticing the drift is part of it too.
Jnana. Knowing, from the root to know. In the Atmabodha, the light that ends the dark of ignorance.
Your line: light, not sweeping, ends the dark. A worry can be a snake, or just a shadow waiting for the light. See you tomorrow.

696.title: Year two close
696.hook: three hundred sixty-five sessions: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the whole Ramayana, a year of festivals, and three paths
696.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
696.howItsDone: Hindus often mark the end of a course of study, or the completion of a text, with a closing recitation, a peace chant, and an offering of thanks to the teacher. Some families sponsor a reading or feed guests when a long recitation is finished.

segments.voice: Yesterday: jnana, and Shankara's Atmabodha. Sweeping won't clear a dark room; only the light does. Today, the last day of year two.

Year two opened with a promise: the texts underneath. Not the stories people tell about Hinduism, but the old pages the stories rest on. Since then you've sat with a father telling his son, that you are. You've read a sage defining yoga in one short line. You've walked the whole Ramayana, from a bird's cry to the earth opening. You've kept a year of festivals. Three hundred sixty-five sessions later, here's the top of the hill, and a look back down the slope.
screen: `THE TEXTS UNDERNEATH.` → `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE SESSIONS.` → `LOOK BACK DOWN THE SLOPE.`

segments.voice: Four blocks. First, the seven big Upanishads: the Chandogya, the Brihadaranyaka, the Taittiriya, the Aitareya, the Prashna, the Mundaka and the Shvetashvatara. Uddalaka and the salt in the water, and his line to Shvetaketu, tat tvam asi, that you are. Gargi asking her questions like arrows. The two kinds of knowledge. Second, the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in four parts, opening with atha, now, and then the definition: yoga is the stilling of the turnings of the mind. Third, Valmiki's Ramayana, seven books in a hundred and eighty sessions: a bow broken, sandals on a throne, a leap across the sea, a homecoming, and a later book whose ending the tradition still argues over with love. Fourth, the festival year, from Janmashtami's midnight to Shivaratri's all-night watch, and then the three strands of the lineage track. Karma, with the Isha asking the mind to remember what was done. Bhakti, with Narada's supreme love and the ache of forgetting. Jnana, with Shankara's light in the dark room. Why call it the summit of the texts? Because so much of what comes next leans on these pages. Later teachers keep returning to the Upanishads. Yoga teachers still go back to Patanjali's sutras. Poets retold Valmiki in other tongues: Kamban in Tamil, Tulsidas in Awadhi. Hindus don't all read these texts the same way, and the schools you met this week read them differently. But they read the same roots. Tomorrow, year three begins with the Mahabharata, and it opens not with a battle but with a king and a sacrifice of snakes.
screen: `SEVEN UPANISHADS: THAT YOU ARE.` · `PATANJALI: STILLING THE MIND.` · `VALMIKI: SEVEN BOOKS.` · `FESTIVALS, AND THREE PATHS.` · then, large: `YOU'VE READ THE ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Sit as if at the top of a hill, the whole year below you, and let one line from year two rise on its own: that you are, the stilling of the mind, remember what was done, or anything else that stayed. When it comes, hold it in the breath, in on the first half, out on the second. Then let it rest, and look out over the year.
Mula. The root: seven Upanishads, the Yoga Sutras, the Ramayana, the festival year, and three paths, all read at the source later teachers keep returning to.
Your line: you've read the roots. The branches come next. Day six hundred ninety-six, and year two is done.

screen: `DAY 696 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ADI PARVA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE FRAME.`

697.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
697.hook: a traveler walks into a forest of sages and says he's come from a king's snake sacrifice, where he heard the whole story
697.carry: a story told beside a fire
697.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
697.howItsDone: In some Hindu homes and temples the Mahabharata is read or recited in parts over many days, with a reciter retelling and explaining each section to listeners. This year follows Kisari Mohan Ganguli's complete English translation, which is in the public domain.

segments.voice: Yesterday: mula, the root, and a look back over year two. Today, year three begins.

A forest called Naimisha. The sages of Shaunaka are keeping a long sacrifice there. A traveler arrives: Ugrashravas, known as Sauti, the son of the storyteller Lomaharshana. They make him welcome and ask what anyone asks a visitor: where have you come from? From the snake sacrifice of King Janamejaya, he says, where he heard a great story told from beginning to end. The sages want all of it. So year three opens the way the Mahabharata opens: not on a battlefield, but in a forest, with someone asking for a story.
screen: `A FOREST, A SACRIFICE, A VISITOR.` → `WHERE HAVE YOU COME FROM?` → `A STORY HEARD AT A KING'S FIRE.`

segments.voice: This is the Adi Parva, the opening book of the Mahabharata. This year we read it a piece at a time, in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English. And before we meet a single hero, the Adi Parva builds a frame. In the forest, Sauti tells the sages what he heard. He heard it at King Janamejaya's sacrifice, told by Vaishampayana, a disciple of Vyasa. And Vyasa, the text says, composed the poem. So the story reaches us hand to hand: Vyasa to his disciple, the disciple to a king, the king's hall to a traveler, the traveler to a forest of sages, and now, through the book, to you. Janamejaya comes from the line of the Pandavas, the heroes of the war to come. His father, King Parikshit, died from the bite of Takshaka, a king of the snakes. Janamejaya answered with a great fire sacrifice meant to draw the snakes into the flames, and at that sacrifice his ancestors' story is told. The whole poem sits inside that picture: a grieving son, a fire built for revenge, and beside the fire, someone telling him how his family's war began. Some readers hear the frame as a question the poem puts to itself from its first pages: what does a man in the middle of vengeance need to hear? Over the next days we walk the frame: a pair of stolen earrings, a snake who speaks for mercy, a bet over a horse's tail, a bird who steals the nectar of the gods, a curse on a king, and a young sage who asks for the fire to stop.
screen: `THE OPENING BOOK.` · `A STORY PASSED HAND TO HAND.` · `A KING'S FATHER, A SNAKE'S BITE.` · `A FIRE BUILT FOR REVENGE.` · then, large: `THE WHOLE POEM SITS INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Notice the circles you sit in: the breath, the body around it, the room and its sounds. Then, wider, the people who handed you the stories you live by, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend at a kitchen table. Let one face come, and let that person sit at the edge of the circle while you breathe.
Adi Parva. The opening book of the Mahabharata, where the whole story is told beside a king's snake sacrifice.
Your line: a story told beside a fire. Tomorrow, a pair of stolen earrings. Day six hundred ninety-seven, and year three is open.

698.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
698.hook: a student loses a queen's earrings to a disguised snake king, and carries the grudge all the way to Janamejaya
698.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
698.howItsDone: Paying a teacher's fee at the end of study, guru dakshina, is a custom some Hindu students still keep, often as a gift or a service the teacher asks for. In the Adi Parva, Uttanka's journey ends at Janamejaya's court, and that is where the snake sacrifice begins to be urged.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Adi Parva opened in a forest, with a traveler and a story first told at King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice. A story told beside a fire.

A student finishes his studies and asks his teacher what fee he can pay. The teacher sends him to ask his wife, and she names it: the earrings worn by the queen of King Paushya, brought back in time for a rite she means to wear them to. The student is Uttanka. The queen gives him the earrings, with a warning: Takshaka, the king of the snakes, wants them badly. Be careful. On the road home, Uttanka sets the earrings down to wash before his prayers. When he looks up, they're gone.
screen: `A STUDENT'S FEE.` → `A QUEEN'S EARRINGS.` → `SET DOWN, AND GONE.`

segments.voice: The thief was a wandering beggar, and as Uttanka chases him, the beggar drops the disguise. It's Takshaka. He slips into a hole in the earth, down into the world of the snakes, and Uttanka follows. What happens down there reads like a dream. Uttanka praises the snakes in verses, and still doesn't get the earrings back. He sees two women at a loom, weaving with black and white threads, a wheel turned by boys, and a man with a horse. The man tells him to blow into the horse, and when he does, smoke and fire pour through the snake world, and a frightened Takshaka hands the earrings back. At home, his teacher explains the figures as gods and powers; the horse, he says, was Agni, fire itself. Uttanka pays his fee in time. Done, you'd think. But Uttanka doesn't let it go. He travels to King Janamejaya and tells him: Takshaka is the one who killed your father. Avenge him. So the snake sacrifice doesn't begin with the king's grief alone. It begins with a student's grudge, carried a long way and set beside someone else's wound. Uttanka has his own score with Takshaka, and he finds a king with a bigger one. That's a question the frame keeps raising: how does anger spread? Not always from the person who was hurt. Sometimes from the one standing next to them, saying, you shouldn't let this go. Janamejaya asks his ministers how his father died. Their answer comes in a few days. First, a snake speaks up for mercy.
screen: `THE BEGGAR WAS TAKSHAKA.` · `DOWN INTO THE SNAKE WORLD.` · `SMOKE AND FIRE; THE EARRINGS BACK.` · `UTTANKA GOES TO THE KING.` · then, large: `HOW DOES ANGER SPREAD?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a grudge you were handed rather than one that began with you: a family feud, a coworker's complaint, an old story about a whole group of people. Set it down in front of you, the way Uttanka set the earrings on the ground, and ask only: whose was it first? You don't have to put it down; just see it clearly, and breathe.
Adi Parva. The opening book, where a student's grudge against a snake king reaches a king's ear.
Your line: how does anger spread? Tomorrow, a bride, a hidden snake and a vow. See you tomorrow.

699.howItsDone: Ahimsa, not harming living beings, is taught in Hindu texts beyond this one, and some Hindus practice it through vegetarian diet, care for animals, and restraint in speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Uttanka, the stolen earrings, and a grudge carried all the way to King Janamejaya. How does anger spread?

The wedding has been set. The bride, Pramadvara, is out with her friends, and she steps on a snake she doesn't see. It bites her, and she dies. The groom is Ruru, a young man of the family of the sage Bhrigu. He goes off alone into the forest and weeps. Then a messenger of the gods comes with an offer: she can live again, if he gives her half of his own life. He gives it. She wakes. They marry. It could end there, happily. It doesn't.
screen: `A BRIDE, A HIDDEN SNAKE.` → `HALF HIS LIFE FOR HERS.` → `IT DOESN'T END THERE.`

segments.voice: Ruru makes a vow: whenever he sees a snake, he will kill it. He carries a heavy stick, and he strikes the snakes he finds. One day he comes on an old snake of a kind called a dundubha, and he raises the stick. The snake speaks. I've done you no harm. Why strike me? A snake killed my wife, Ruru answers, so I kill snakes. The dundubha says: we're not the ones who bite. We share the name snake with them, and nothing else. Then it tells him who it really is: a sage, cursed to live in this shape until the day it met him. Standing as a man again, the sage teaches Ruru. Not harming living beings is the highest dharma. A man of a priestly family should be known for gentleness and forgiveness, not for the stick. Notice where the Adi Parva puts this. We're inside the frame of a king trying to burn the snakes, and before we reach that fire, the poem lets a creature in a snake's shape speak for ahimsa, not harming. Ruru's grief was real. His rage was real. But he had turned one bite into a war on a whole kind of creature. The sage even points ahead to Janamejaya's snake sacrifice, and says it was stopped. Then he's gone. Ruru goes home and asks his father to tell him the rest, and that's how the poem gets us back to the fire.
screen: `RURU'S VOW: KILL EVERY SNAKE.` · `WE'RE NOT THE ONES WHO BITE.` · `A SAGE UNDER A CURSE.` · `NOT HARMING: THE HIGHEST DHARMA.` · then, large: `AHIMSA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hurt that came from one person or one thing, and notice whether it has spread: from one dog to all dogs, one driver to all drivers, one person to everyone who looks like them. Don't argue with it; just see the line between the one that bit and the ones that never did. Breathe in on the one, and out on the many.

700.title: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
700.hook: two sisters bet on the color of a horse's tail, and one wins by sending her snake sons to cheat
700.carry: the curse fell on the innocent
700.tomorrow: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame
700.howItsDone: In some regions Hindu families honor snakes, nagas, at the festival of Nag Panchami. In the Adi Parva, Kadru's curse is the snakes' own family story: why the fire was coming for them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ruru's stick, and a harmless snake who taught him not to harm. We share the name, nothing else.

What color is a white horse's tail? That's the bet between two sisters, Kadru and Vinata, both wives of the sage Kashyapa. They've just seen a marvelous white horse, Uchchaihshravas, which rose from the churning of the ocean. Vinata says the horse is white all over. Kadru says its tail is black. The stakes are steep: the loser becomes the winner's slave. They agree to go and look. Before they do, Kadru calls her sons. Her sons are snakes.
screen: `A WHITE HORSE FROM THE OCEAN.` → `A BET ON ITS TAIL.` → `THE LOSER BECOMES A SLAVE.`

segments.voice: Kadru tells them: go and hang on the horse's tail like black hairs, so I win. Some of them refuse. And Kadru, furious, curses the ones who refuse: they will burn in the fire of a snake sacrifice held by a king named Janamejaya. That's the line the whole frame hangs on. The fire we met on the first day was spoken over these snakes long before Janamejaya was born. The text adds a hard detail. Brahma, the creator, hears the curse and lets it stand, because the snakes, the text says, had become fierce and poisonous, a danger to other creatures. So a mother's curse becomes part of a larger order. Then the bet plays out. The tail looks black, Vinata loses, and she becomes her sister's slave. Kadru wins by a trick. And look who the curse falls on: not the cheat, but the sons who said no to cheating. The text doesn't explain that away or soften it. It leaves the unfairness on the page, with the creator's assent beside it, and lets the listener feel how uneasy that is. In Sanskrit, Janamejaya's rite is the sarpasatra, the snake sacrifice, and its fire will come long afterward, lit by a king who thinks only of his father. One more thread starts here. Vinata has a son still to come out of his egg, a great bird. He'll be the one to set her free.
screen: `HANG ON THE TAIL LIKE BLACK HAIRS.` · `A CURSE ON THE SONS WHO REFUSED.` · `BRAHMA LETS IT STAND.` · `VINATA LOSES, AND SERVES.` · then, large: `SARPASATRA: THE SNAKE SACRIFICE.`

segments.voice: Remember a time someone asked you to help them win by bending something: cover for them, shade a number, take their side before you knew the facts. Don't grade what you did; just notice how the asking felt in the chest, the jaw, the hands. Breathe in and feel that pull, then breathe out into the room where a no can live.
